authority_sources.title: Exudative Epidermitis in Pigs
explicit_dis050_support: Merck describes exudative epidermitis as a generalized staphylococcal infection affecting young pigs.
Merck states that lesions are caused by Staphylococcus hyicus, while other staphylococci have been sporadically implicated.
Merck states that the disease occurs in pigs 5-60 days old, with the acute form usually affecting suckling piglets and a chronic form more common in weaned pigs.
Merck describes early clinical signs as listlessness and reddening of skin, followed by moist greasy exudate and nonpruritic lesions.
Merck states that diagnosis is usually presumptive based on clinical signs and that bacterial culture of lesions can be used when confirmation is necessary or when an isolate is desired.
Merck lists differential diagnoses including sarcoptic mange, nutritional deficiency diseases such as parakeratosis, ringworm, and pityriasis rosea.
Merck states that treatment selection should be guided by antimicrobial culture and susceptibility testing when antimicrobials are used.

supported_claims.claim: Merck identifies exudative epidermitis in pigs as a generalized staphylococcal infection; lesions are caused by Staphylococcus hyicus, while other staphylococci have been sporadically implicated.
Merck states that exudative epidermitis occurs in pigs 5-60 days old; acute disease usually affects suckling piglets and chronic disease is more common in weaned pigs.
Merck describes early signs as listlessness and reddening of the skin, followed by rapid spread of moist greasy exudate and nonpruritic lesions.
Merck states that abrasions or lacerations precede infection and that immunity, hygiene, nutrition, mange mites, and other skin-damaging factors can affect severity and progression.
Merck states that presumptive diagnosis is usually based on clinical signs, with bacterial culture of lesions used when confirmation is necessary or when an isolate is desired.
Merck lists differential diagnoses including sarcoptic mange, nutritional deficiency diseases including parakeratosis, ringworm, and pityriasis rosea.
Merck states that antimicrobial treatment selection should be guided by antimicrobial culture and susceptibility testing; this supports a treatment-boundary fact, not a standalone prescription.
